transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello. I suppose I’m here because my regular doctor—Dr. Miller, I’ve been seeing him for over a decade, nice man but he does tend to fret over the smallest things—he seems incredibly concerned that my meal planning has gotten, well, he called it "too tight." 

But honestly, I just don't see it that way at all. I work as an operations research analyst, you see, so looking at systems and finding the most efficient, structured way to do things is literally how my brain works all day long. I analyze variables for a living! So to me, my eating habits just feel like keeping a sensible routine. I keep breakfast to just a yogurt—usually just a small plain one, it's quick, there's no fuss, no messy cleanup before I have to log on for work. 

And then, well, if I’m busy during the day, which I almost always am with my project deadlines and the endless meetings, I just skip lunch. It’s just easier to push through than to break my concentration and figure out food in the middle of a complex data model. Then when I get to the evening, I make a very measured dinner. I like to portion it out exactly, knowing precisely what's on the plate, just to make sure the day stays orderly and predictable. I tried to explain to Dr. Miller that it’s just about maintaining a sense of order in my schedule, especially at my age, but he just wouldn't let it go and insisted I come see you. So... here I am, taking up your time with my perfectly logical routine.
Have you lost a noticeable amount of weight recently, or do you have concerns about your weight or body shape that influence how you eat?

Well, yes, I suppose my weight has drifted down, which is exactly what got Dr. Miller so worked up in the first place. He had his nurse weigh me—which, by the way, they always do right after I’ve had my morning coffee and still have my heavy cardigan on, so the data is already slightly skewed if you ask me. But yes, the number on the scale has gone down more than he likes. He showed me the trajectory on his little chart, pointing out the downward slope over the last several months. 

But when I look at that same chart, I don't see a crisis. I see a trend line, and honestly... I still find myself thinking that a little lower would be, well, just a cleaner number. A more manageable baseline, if you will. It’s like when you’re optimizing a supply chain model; you want to trim the excess until you find the absolute most efficient operating point. And when I look in the mirror, or when I feel how my clothes fit—I just think there’s still room for optimization. It just feels better, lighter, when the number is lower. It’s not about vanity, really, it’s about precision. If I can maintain a lower number, it just proves that my system is working, that I have everything under control. So yes, I’ve lost weight, but I really don't see why it's such a cause for alarm when it just feels like I'm finally getting the variables aligned perfectly.
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

Well, no, not really. I mean, "depressed" is such a strong word, isn't it? It implies a sort of... functional breakdown, a failure of the system to operate, and I am certainly still operating. I get up at 5:30 every morning, exactly as I always have. I make my coffee—pour-over, exactly 18 grams of beans, because the drip machines just don't extract the flavor properly—and I sit down at my desk by 6:00 to review the overnight data runs. 

I suppose... well, I will admit that I don't go out to dinner with my colleagues anymore. We used to do that, you know, on the third Thursday of every month, a little group of us from the analytics division. We'd go to this Italian place downtown. But it just became so... inefficient. And stressful, frankly. You can't control the portion sizes at a restaurant, you don't know how much butter or oil they're using in the kitchen, the variables are entirely hidden from the end user. It drove me absolutely up the wall trying to calculate the input values for a simple plate of pasta. So I stopped going. 

But I wouldn't call that losing interest, exactly. It's more of a strategic reallocation of my time. Why spend two hours sitting in a noisy restaurant, dealing with all that unpredictable data, when I can stay home, have my measured dinner, and read a good book on queuing theory? It’s just a preference for order. I still enjoy my work immensely, I still enjoy my quiet evenings. I just... I prefer things to be contained. Predictable. I don't feel sad about it, I just feel like I've streamlined my social life the same way I've streamlined my schedule. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm depressed at all. Just highly organized.
Do you feel anxious or upset if something interrupts your usual eating schedule or if you're unable to control your food portions exactly as you'd planned?

Well, "anxious" is... it's a broad term, isn't it? But if we're talking about the data getting skewed, then yes, I suppose I do have a rather strong reaction. It’s not so much about the schedule being interrupted—though I do prefer my 6:00 PM dinner time, it's optimal for digestion before bed—but it’s really about the inputs and the outcomes. 

For instance, if I do happen to eat something that I haven't perfectly measured, or heaven forbid I am forced into a situation like a restaurant meal where the variables are entirely out of my hands, the next morning is... well, it's highly stressful. If I step on the scale—which I do every morning at exactly 6:15, right after the bathroom and before the coffee, to ensure consistent data collection—and the number is up even a single pound... oh, it’s just awful. It’s this sharp, sudden panic, right in my chest. It feels like a complete system failure. It tells me that I’ve completely lost control of the model, that the parameters have breached acceptable limits. 

And when that happens, I just... I can't let it stand. I have to correct it immediately. The whole next day becomes about recalibration. I'll cut back the dinner portion even further, maybe skip the yogurt at breakfast entirely, just to get the numbers back in line. It’s not that I’m trying to be difficult, it’s just that when the data spikes like that, it feels like everything is unraveling, and I simply must tighten the controls to fix it. So yes, I do get quite upset if the portions aren't exact, because the consequences on the scale are just... they're unacceptable to me. I need the trend line to stay steady, or ideally, continue its downward optimization.
When you feel like your eating has gotten out of control or that you've consumed something you didn't plan for, do you ever make yourself sick, use laxatives, or exercise excessively to compensate?

Well, no, I don't do anything like that. Making myself sick... well, that just seems incredibly disruptive to the body's natural equilibrium, doesn't it? It's a violent reaction, and as I've mentioned, I am looking for stability and precision, not chaos. And laxatives, well, they just artificially manipulate the water weight and the digestive timeline, which would completely ruin the integrity of my morning data collection. You wouldn't know what was a true variable shift and what was just chemical interference. 

As for exercise... I mean, I do have a routine, of course. I walk for exactly forty-five minutes every evening after dinner, at a brisk pace of about 3.5 miles per hour. It’s good for cardiovascular health, and it aids in the digestion process I mentioned earlier. But I wouldn't call it excessive. I don't go to the gym and run on a treadmill for hours until I drop, if that's what you mean. That sort of extreme physical exertion just isn't sustainable for a long-term operational model. It introduces too much wear and tear on the system, especially at my age. 

So, no, if there's a... a deviation from the plan, as I said, my method of correction is simply to adjust the input variables the following day. I reduce the caloric intake, I tighten the parameters. I don't try to force the system to purge the error; I just recalibrate the future inputs to smooth out the trend line. It’s much more logical, really. Why create a secondary crisis by making yourself ill when you can just adjust the formula and achieve the same result through disciplined management?
Do you have a strong fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though you are currently at a lower weight?

Well, "fear" is an interesting word. I suppose, yes, if you want to use that terminology, though I tend to view it more as a critical aversion to system degradation. But as I was just explaining a moment ago about my morning weigh-ins... if that scale is up even a single pound—just one pound, mind you, which some might argue is a normal fluctuation, but in data analysis, a sudden unexplained spike is never something you just ignore—if it's up after, say, a normal dinner or one of those dreadful restaurant meals I mentioned, I do feel this... this incredibly sharp panic. 

It’s a very physical sensation, actually. My heart rate elevates, I can feel the adrenaline and cortisol flooding my system right there in the bathroom, and it’s this overwhelming, undeniable realization that I have completely lost control of the variables. 

And to me, gaining weight, becoming "fat" as you put it... well, that represents the ultimate operational failure, doesn't it? It means the inputs have vastly exceeded the necessary energy requirements for optimal output, resulting in excess storage. It’s inefficient. It’s sloppy. I have spent thirty-five years of my life optimizing supply chains and logistics networks to eliminate excess, to trim the fat, quite literally, from corporate budgets and routing schedules. So to allow my own physical vessel to accumulate excess mass... it goes against every fundamental principle I believe in. 

That panic I feel when the scale ticks upward, it’s not just vanity. I don't care about looking like a magazine cover, I'm sixty-three years old for heaven's sake, my concerns are entirely structural. It's about the integrity of the model. When I see that number go up, all I can think is that the parameters are breached, the system is compromised, and I absolutely need to correct it the very next day. I have to dial back the inputs immediately to get the trend line back to baseline. So, yes, if you want to call it a strong fear, I suppose I am terrified of the number going up, because it means I've failed at the basic, foundational management of my own body. I just can't tolerate that kind of error.

There is no evidence of compulsive behaviors seen in F42 or mood symptoms suggesting F43.2. The clinical picture aligns specifically with anorexia nervosa (F50.00).
